publicTrace: Base rate reference class: SPM child poverty post-ARPA expansion (2022–2024) averaged approximately 13.2 pct, with the 2024 published rate at 13.4 pct and a year-over-year change of -0.3 pct. The post-expansion era (2022 onward, after the temporary CTC boost expired) provides the most relevant reference class for 2025 current-law conditions.

Point estimate mechanism: A weighted blend of the PolicyEngine current-law prior (13.0 pct, weight 0.55), post-expansion Census SPM history (13.2 pct, weight 0.35), and the latest published 2024 rate (13.4 pct, weight 0.10), minus a small macro adjustment (-0.05 pct), yields a calibrated point estimate of approximately 13.0 pct. This reflects no major new child-benefit expansions under current law for 2025.

Uncertainty widening: The 80% interval spans roughly 11.3–14.6 pct. The lower tail reflects possible upside from SNAP, Medicaid, or EITC expansions not yet captured; the upper tail reflects SNAP benefit cliffs, rising MOOP costs, or housing cost increases that SPM captures but official poverty does not.

Disconfirming consideration (lower outcome): If Congress enacted or extended refundable CTC provisions or SNAP expansions effective in 2025 that PolicyEngine's current-law snapshot did not capture, the rate could fall below 11.9 pct, outside the stated interval.

Disconfirming consideration (higher outcome): If medical out-of-pocket expenses rose sharply, housing costs increased faster than SPM thresholds, or SNAP caseloads declined due to work-requirement enforcement, the rate could exceed 14.3 pct, outside the stated interval.

Asymmetry note: The distribution is left-skewed relative to the point estimate because the post-expansion floor appears sticky near 13 pct under current law, but upside risk from cost pressures is somewhat fatter-tailed than downside risk from new transfers.

Data availability caveat: The Census SPM tables page was reachable but no machine-readable 2025 data exists yet; PolicyEngine input confirms current-law status but is not a fresh microsimulation run. Uncertainty is explicitly widened to account for these data-path limitations.
assumptions: Current law for 2025 includes no new major child-benefit expansions beyond those already in effect in 2024 (no expanded CTC, no new universal child allowance).
The SPM methodology remains consistent with recent years, including geographic housing cost adjustments, MOOP deductions, and tax/transfer imputations.
ASEC sampling variability contributes approximately ±0.3–0.5 pct standard error to the published rate, which is incorporated into the interval width.
Macro conditions in 2025 (employment, wages, inflation) are broadly similar to 2024, with no severe recession or major labor market shock.
dataCaveats: The Census SPM data tables page was fetched live but contains no 2025 data; the historical series used here is a prototype seed, not a machine-readable Census API endpoint.
The PolicyEngine input confirms current-law policy status (id=2, label='Current law') but is not a fresh server-side microsimulation run for 2025; the stored prior of 13.0 pct is used as a seed.
SPM estimates are sensitive to MOOP, housing cost thresholds, and geographic price indices, which can diverge from CPI trends and introduce volatility not captured by the calibration prior.
Year-to-year SPM revisions (methodology updates, weight adjustments) can shift the series by 0.2–0.5 pct independently of policy or economic changes.
drivers: Refundable tax credit generosity (EITC, CTC) under current law for tax year 2025
SNAP benefit levels and caseload changes affecting food resource counts in SPM
Medical out-of-pocket expense trends affecting SPM resource deductions
Housing cost growth relative to SPM geographic threshold updates
Labor market conditions affecting earned income and payroll tax offsets in SPM resources
